title: The early days of oil production

paragraphs.text: In the 1850s, geologists and chemists in Europe and North America were looking for something better for lighting fuel than whale oil. The numbers of whales were falling, and their oil could no longer supply the demands of the rapidly growing cities. Chemists in Britain, Europe and North America refined fuel for lamps from coal asphalt and turpentine, the coal-oils abrasive.

In 1854, Abraham Gesner, a Canadian geologist, obtained a colourless oil from asphalt in 1854 and called it kerosene, combining the Greek words for wax and oil. By 1859, he had a plant in New York producing 5,000 gallons a day. More than 30 other companies in America were soon manufacturing similar products.

Travelling through Pennsylvania, George Bissell, a poorly paid American journalist and teacher, saw villagers in Oil Creek collecting a sticky black fluid which bubbled from the ground. They spread cloths to sponge it up and sold it to pharmacists, who prescribed it for headaches, worms, rheumatism, and the sores on horses’ backs. Bissell reckoned that this ‘rock oil’, as it was called, could be refined and sold as lamp fuel and machine lubricant. He gathered a group of like-minded businessmen to raise money for research and they paid Benjamin Silliman, a chemist, to evaluate the oil. In 1855, Silliman declared a valuable lighting fuel, and backed his opinion by putting money into the new Pennsylvania Rock Oil Company. All the company had to do now was to find an oil well. It recruited Edwin Drake, an unemployed railway conductor to prospect near a timber camp called Titusville in the hills of north-west Pennsylvania. However, after more than a year he had found nothing, and his masters wrote to him and told him to stop.

The letter was already on its way when, in August 1859, Drake drilled to just over 30 metres and struck oil. As it was being transferred to tubs and barrels, the news prompted the first oil rush. Thousands of adventurers, men and women, hurried to Titusville, where so much oil was gushing that there were not enough barrels to hold it. In fact, barrels were more costly than the oil itself.

By 1860, 75 wells were working in America’s first oilfield, and the product was refined and marketed as kerosene. So much oil was available that the price fell in a few months from ten dollars a barrel to ten cents. The teams of drivers who steered oil wagon down the muddy tracks out of Titusville demanded big fees. The bosses defeated them by building the first pipeline, a wooden tube, to take the oil away; but not before the drivers tried sabotage and gunfire in an attempt to get their way. In 1861, a cargo of Pennsylvania kerosene in barrels was stowed aboard a London-bound sailing ship. Terrified of explosion, the crew fled. The captain toured the waterfront looking for other people to crew the ship. He sailed before they realised what the cargo was. Within five years, American oil exports to Britain were worth around $15 million.

In 1865, John Davison Rockefeller, a ruthless, twenty-six-year-old businessman became an oil refiner in Cleveland, Ohio. At thirty he founded Standard Oil and had 25 refineries. By the end of the 1870s, the company had acquired nine-tenths of American refining, and all the oil wagons of the Pennsylvania Railroad. He shaped the modern oil industry and was one of the wealthiest men on earth. But at the age of sixty, feeling the first symptoms of arthritis, he turned philanthropist and gave more than $500 million to medical research. He died at the age of ninety-eight.

In 1892, the mighty Rockefeller company was shaken by the actions of trader Marcus Samuel, from the East End of London. Standard Oil sent kerosene in sailing ships to South East Asia, via the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. A much faster and cheaper route was through the Suez Canal in Egypt, but the authorities there had banned the transport of Standard’s oil for fear of explosion. Samuel, however, saw that by buying kerosene from Baku, a city on the Caspian Sea in what was then Russia, and shipping it through Suez, he would be able to undercut Standard. To do the job he needed a fleet of special tankers designed to pass the canal authority’s safety tests. The first of his fleet, Murex, was thus designed to minimise the risk of explosion. It also had tanks that could be steam-cleaned to permit the transport of sugar on the return voyage.

Murex succeeded in reaching the required standard for safety. It sailed from England to Batumi on the Black Sea, was loaded with 4,000 tonnes of kerosene brought by rail from Baku, and shipped it through Suez to Singapore and Bangkok. It was a triumph. Samuel had already built a network of storage tanks in South East Asia and now he was ready to exploit a huge new market. Standard supplied blue oil cans for customers to carry their kerosene home in, and Samuel hastily ordered tonnes of Welsh tin to be sent to the East and made into bright red cans. By the end of 1893, he and his brother Sam had a fleet of 11 tankers, all given the names of seashells in honour of the pattern their merchant father favoured for some of his merchandise. In 1897, they founded Shell. By 1902, nine-tenths of the oil passing through Suez went in this company’s ships.

questions.prompt: Urban growth created the need for a replacement for whale oil.
The scientist who first extracted kerosene was uninterested in its manufacture.
Many of the claims regarding the health benefits of rock oil were unproven.
Benjamin Silliman believed so strongly in rock oil that he invested in it.
Edwin Drake located oil much more quickly than his employers had expected.
In the last part of the 1850s, Pennsylvanian oil was less expensive than the containers it was stored in.
The construction of a pipeline was resisted by the men who transported oil barrels.

groups.sourceInstructions: Question 8 – 13 Answer the questions below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 8-13 on your answer sheet.

questions.prompt: Which company did John Davison Rockefeller establish?
Besides his oil refining company, what else did Rockefeller own?
For what purpose did Rockefeller donate money when he was older?
What could Samuel’s tankers carry on their way back from South East Asia?
What were Samuel’s red kerosene containers made from?
After which objects did Samuel name his ships?
